lessons.title: Common African Herbs for Tea: Rooibos, Hibiscus, Moringa, Lemongrass
lessons.body:
Start with four herbs that grow well across much of Africa and sell reliably at markets. Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) is a South African shrub grown mainly in the Cederberg region. It needs sandy, acidic soil and winter rainfall. You harvest the needle-like leaves and fine stems, then ferment them in heaps for 8 to 12 hours to get the deep red colour and sweet, woody flavour. Unfermented green rooibos is also sold at a higher price. A small plot of 100 plants can yield 20 to 30 kg of dried tea per year.

Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa), called zobo or bissap in West Africa, is grown from seed in warm, dry conditions. The calyces, not the petals, are what you dry and brew. Harvest 3 to 4 weeks after flowering, when the calyces are fleshy and bright red. Sun-dry them for 3 to 5 days on clean mats until brittle. One hectare can produce 500 to 800 kg of dried calyces. Hibiscus is tart and high in vitamin C, so it blends well with ginger or pineapple peel.

Moringa (Moringa oleifera) is a fast-growing tree that tolerates poor soil and drought. For tea, harvest young leaves, strip them from stems, and dry them in the shade for 2 to 3 days. Shade drying keeps the leaves green and preserves vitamins. Do not boil moringa leaves; pour hot water at about 80 degrees Celsius over 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaf and steep for 3 minutes. Moringa is bitter if over-steeped, so measure carefully.

Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) grows in clumps and spreads easily. Cut stalks 15 to 20 cm above the ground every 6 to 8 weeks. You can use fresh stalks or dry them in bundles for 1 to 2 weeks. Lemongrass is a good starter crop because it needs little water and few inputs. For a small tea business, plant at least 50 clumps so you can harvest continuously. Always label your dried herbs with the harvest date and location. Buyers pay more when they can trust the source and the quality.

lessons.title: Where to Find Herbs: Wild Harvesting, Farms, and Markets
lessons.body:
You have three main sources for tea herbs: wild harvesting, farms, and markets. Each has different costs, risks, and quality levels. Choose based on what you can control and what your customers will pay.

Wild harvesting is cheapest but riskiest. In many parts of Africa, common tea herbs grow along roadsides, riverbanks, and bushland. Lemongrass often grows near water. Hibiscus and rooibos are usually cultivated, not wild. Moringa grows in villages and towns. Before harvesting wild plants, get permission from the landowner or local authority. Never harvest from roadsides where exhaust and herbicides contaminate plants. Avoid areas near mines, rubbish dumps, or spraying programmes. Take only 1 in 3 plants from a wild patch so it can regrow. Record the GPS location or a clear landmark so you can return.

Farms give you consistent quality and volume. Visit smallholder farms within 50 to 100 km of your processing site. Ask what they grow, when they harvest, and how they dry. A good farm keeps records of planting dates and drying methods. Offer to buy a fixed quantity at a fair price before harvest. For example, agree on 50 kg of dried hibiscus calyces at a set price per kg. This gives the farmer income security and gives you reliable supply. If you can, visit during harvest to check the crop yourself.

Markets are the fastest way to buy herbs, but quality varies. In cities like Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, and Johannesburg, you can find dried hibiscus, moringa powder, and lemongrass in bulk. Bring a small scale, a clean container, and a moisture meter if you have one. Check for mould, dust, insects, and strong off-smells. Ask the trader where the herb came from and how old it is. Fresh dried herbs should smell strong and look bright, not faded or grey.

For a small tea business, start by buying from one or two trusted farms and one reliable market trader. Build a simple supplier list with name, phone number, herb, price, and quality notes. This makes it easy to reorder and to compare prices as you grow.

lessons.title: How to Identify Herbs Safely and Avoid Toxic Plants
lessons.body:
Misidentifying a plant can make your customers sick or kill them. You must learn to identify herbs with certainty before you sell any tea. Use three tools: a local plant guide, a knowledgeable elder or extension officer, and your own senses. Never rely on one tool alone.

Start with leaves. Rooibos has fine, needle-like green leaves on a low shrub. Hibiscus has broad, lobed leaves with serrated edges and red stems. Moringa has small, oval leaflets arranged along a long stem, and the whole leaf looks feathery. Lemongrass has long, sharp-edged blades that smell strongly of lemon when crushed. If a plant looks similar but smells wrong, do not use it. Smell is one of your best safety checks.

Learn the dangerous lookalikes in your area. In many African regions, the toxic plant known as "wild castor" or "mkakati" has leaves that can be confused with hibiscus. Some species of Solanum (nightshade) have leaves similar to moringa but produce toxic berries. Datura, also called jimsonweed, has large leaves and trumpet flowers and is highly poisonous. If you are not 100% sure, throw the plant away. There is no tea worth a hospital visit.

Use a simple identification checklist for every new plant. First, confirm the leaf shape and arrangement. Second, crush a leaf and smell it. Third, check the stem, flowers, and fruit if present. Fourth, compare with a photo in a trusted guide such as "Medicinal Plants of East Africa" or a local extension pamphlet. Fifth, ask two experienced people to confirm. Only then harvest a small test batch.

When you harvest, keep each herb in a separate labelled bag. Never mix unknown plants with known ones. Wear gloves if you are handling sap. Wash your hands after harvesting. If you plan to sell, keep a written record of who identified the plant and when. This protects you and builds trust with buyers. Teach your workers the same rules. A safe tea business is a lasting tea business.

lessons.title: Sustainable Harvesting Practices for Small Businesses
lessons.body:
Sustainable harvesting means taking herbs in a way that lets the plant and the ecosystem recover. If you strip a wild patch bare, you will have nothing to sell next season. Good practices also improve quality and reduce waste.

For leafy herbs like moringa and lemongrass, never cut more than one-third of the plant at a time. For moringa, harvest only the young stems and leaves, leaving the main trunk and at least half the canopy. Wait 4 to 6 weeks before harvesting the same tree again. For lemongrass, cut stalks 15 to 20 cm above the ground and leave the base to regrow. You can harvest the same clump every 6 to 8 weeks for years if you do not pull it up.

For hibiscus, harvest only the mature red calyces and leave the green ones to develop. Pick in the cool of the morning. Do not uproot the plant. Hibiscus is an annual in many areas, so save some seed for the next season. For rooibos, harvest in summer when the bushes are 18 months to 3 years old. Cut the stems 30 cm above the ground. The plant will regrow, but it needs a rest period. Never harvest rooibos from the same bush two years in a row.

Wild harvesting needs extra care. Follow the "one in three" rule: for every three plants you find, harvest only one. Leave the strongest plants to seed. Use a sharp knife or secateurs, not a machete that damages the plant. Fill your basket loosely so leaves do not crush. Walk lightly and avoid trampling young plants. If a patch is small, skip it and find a larger one.

Record what you harvest. Write the date, location, herb, and amount in a notebook. This helps you rotate harvest sites and avoid overuse. It also shows buyers that you manage your supply responsibly. Some buyers pay a premium for herbs harvested sustainably. You can also plant your own herb garden to reduce pressure on wild areas. A 10 m by 10 m plot of lemongrass and moringa can supply a small tea business year-round.

lessons.title: Building Relationships with Local Herb Suppliers
lessons.body:
Your tea business depends on reliable suppliers. A good relationship with farmers and market traders is worth more than a one-time low price. Treat suppliers as partners, not as people to squeeze.

Start by visiting in person. Go to the farm or market stall during a quiet time. Introduce yourself, explain what you make, and ask about their herbs. Listen more than you talk. Find out their harvest calendar, their main challenges, and what price they need to make a fair profit. Take notes. Ask if you can call them before each harvest to reserve quantity. For example, agree to buy 20 kg of dried hibiscus every month for six months.

Pay fairly and pay on time. If you agree on a price, pay it without haggling after delivery. If you can, pay a deposit before harvest so the farmer can buy inputs. This builds trust and secures your supply. When you receive herbs, check quality immediately. If there is a problem, discuss it calmly and agree on a solution. Do not humiliate a supplier in front of others. A farmer who feels respected will save the best herbs for you.

Communicate clearly about quality. Show your supplier a sample of the dried herb you want: bright colour, strong smell, no mould, no stems or stones. Explain how you will use it. If you need shade-dried moringa, say so. If you need hibiscus calyces without seed pods, say so. Give feedback after each delivery. A simple message like "The last batch was excellent, please keep the same drying method" goes a long way.

Build a network of at least three suppliers for each herb. If one has a bad season, you can buy from another. Keep a simple supplier book with names, phone numbers, herbs, prices, and quality ratings. Visit them at least twice a year. Bring small gifts or share your tea samples. Over time, you can sign simple written agreements. This protects both sides and helps you plan your production with confidence.

lessons.title: Storing Fresh Herbs to Maintain Quality
lessons.body:
Poor storage destroys more tea than bad harvesting. Heat, light, air, and moisture make herbs lose colour, flavour, and medicinal value. You need to dry herbs properly, then store them in the right containers and conditions.

Drying comes first. Spread herbs in a single layer on clean drying racks or mats. Use shade for moringa and lemongrass to keep them green. Use full sun for hibiscus and rooibos to develop colour. Turn the herbs every few hours. Drying takes 2 to 5 days depending on the herb and weather. The herb is ready when it snaps, not bends. If it feels leathery, it is not dry enough. Aim for less than 10 percent moisture. A simple moisture meter costs about 20 to 50 US dollars and pays for itself quickly.

Once dry, cool the herbs completely before packing. Warm herbs create condensation inside the container. Pack in clean, dry, food-grade containers. Glass jars with airtight lids work well for small quantities. For bulk, use food-grade plastic buckets with sealing lids or double-lined paper sacks inside a plastic outer bag. Never use old fertiliser or chemical bags. Label every container with the herb name, harvest date, and location.

Store in a cool, dark, dry place. Ideal temperature is 15 to 25 degrees Celsius. Keep away from sunlight, stoves, and damp walls. Humidity should be below 60 percent. If you live in a humid area, add a small silica gel packet or a clean piece of dry charcoal to each container. Check stored herbs every two weeks. Look for mould, insects, or fading colour. If you see mould, throw the whole batch away. Do not try to wash or re-dry mouldy herbs.

For a small business, use the first-in, first-out rule. Sell older stock before newer stock. Keep a storage log with dates and quantities. Properly stored dried herbs keep their quality for 12 to 18 months. Moringa leaf powder is best within 6 months. Hibiscus and rooibos can last 2 years if kept dry and dark. Good storage protects your reputation and reduces waste.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sourcing and Identifying Local Herbs

This practical reference is built for small African tea and infusion businesses that need reliable, repeatable herb sourcing. Whether you are blending rooibos for export, drying hibiscus for local retail, or adding moringa and lemongrass to a health-focused product line, the quality of your raw material determines your price point, shelf life, and customer trust. Use this guide as a working document: print it, annotate it, and take it with you to farms, markets, and wild harvesting sites.

Common African Herbs for Tea: What to Buy and Why

Africa's tea herb market is anchored by a handful of high-demand species. Each has distinct sourcing economics, quality markers, and buyer expectations.

Table 1: Key African Tea Herbs â Sourcing and Quality Indicators
Herb Main African Sources Key Quality Marker Typical Buyer Use
Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) Western Cape, South Africa (Cederberg region) Reddish-brown needle-like leaves; sweet, woody aroma; low tannin Premium caffeine-free blends, export retail
Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa) Nigeria, Sudan, Senegal, Mali, Egypt Deep red calyces; tart flavor; high anthocyanin color Zobo drinks, iced tea, vitamin C claims
Moringa (Moringa oleifera) Kenya, Ghana, Nigeria, Malawi, Tanzania Bright green dried leaf; earthy-green aroma; no yellowing Nutritional infusions, wellness blends
Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ghana, Rwanda Strong citrus aroma; pale green stalks; firm, not limp Digestive teas, flavor blends, retail packs

Sources: FAO, Non-Wood Forest Products: Medicinal Plants; CBI (Centre for the Promotion of Imports), Exporting Rooibos to Europe; and national agriculture extension reports from Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa.

Where to Find Herbs: Wild Harvesting, Farms, and Markets

Your sourcing channel shapes cost, traceability, and risk. Wild harvesting is cheapest but hardest to verify; farms offer consistency but higher prices; markets are convenient but often lack provenance. For a small business, the best strategy is usually a hybrid: one or two reliable farm suppliers for core volume, plus wild or market sourcing for seasonal or specialty herbs.

Table 2: Sourcing Channel Comparison for Small Tea Businesses
Channel Cost per kg (indicative) Traceability Best For Main Risk
Wild harvesting Low (labor only) Low Seasonal herbs, pilot batches Misidentification, overharvesting, land access disputes
Smallholder farms Medium MediumâHigh Core volume, consistent quality Pesticide use, seasonal shortfalls
Commercial estates High High Export-grade, certification needs Minimum order quantities, price volatility
Local markets LowâMedium Low Top-up, testing new herbs Adulteration, unknown drying methods

Sources: CBI market data; FAO Non-Wood Forest Products series; and field interviews summarized in African herbal trade reports.

How to Identify Herbs Safely and Avoid Toxic Plants

Misidentification is the single biggest safety risk in herbal tea production. Several toxic plants resemble common tea herbs. For example, Datura stramonium (jimsonweed) can be mistaken for edible leafy herbs, and some Solanum species resemble moringa seedlings. Never harvest a plant you cannot identify with certainty.

Use a three-step verification: (1) identify using at least two independent sources (a local botanist, extension officer, or illustrated guide); (2) confirm with a second experienced harvester; (3) test a small batch before commercial use. Keep a photo log of every plant you harvest, including leaves, flowers, and stems.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Toxic Lookalikes

Never harvest or sell a herb you cannot identify with 100% certainty. Toxic plants such as Datura (jimsonweed), Nerium oleander, and certain Solanum species can contaminate tea batches and cause serious illness or death. Symptoms of poisoning include nausea, blurred vision, rapid heartbeat, confusion, and seizures.

  • Do not harvest from roadsides, industrial areas, or sprayed fields.
  • Do not buy dried herbs from markets unless the vendor can name the species and source.
  • If a customer reports illness after consuming your product, stop sales immediately and contact local health authorities.
  • Keep a sample of every batch for at least 6 months for traceability.

Sustainable Harvesting Practices for Small Businesses

Sustainability is not just ethical â it is commercial. Buyers in Europe, North America, and increasingly within Africa ask for proof of sustainable sourcing. Overharvesting destroys your future supply and can lead to local restrictions or community conflict.

  • Harvest no more than 30% of a wild plant population in any season. Leave enough for regeneration.
  • Take only the plant part you need. For lemongrass, cut stalks; do not uproot. For hibiscus, pick mature calyces and leave the plant to produce more.
  • Rotate harvest zones so no area is stripped year after year.
  • Harvest at the right time. Lemongrass is most aromatic in the morning; hibiscus calyces are best when fully red but before they dry on the plant.
  • Work with community agreements. If you harvest on communal land, get permission and share benefits â this protects your access and reputation.

Building Relationships with Local Herb Suppliers

Your supplier is a business partner, not just a vendor. Strong relationships give you priority during shortages, better prices, and early warning about quality issues. Treat suppliers professionally:

  • Pay on time. Smallholder farmers often lack working capital; late payment damages trust and supply.
  • Be clear about quality standards. Show farmers what good dried hibiscus or moringa looks like. Provide simple grading examples.
  • Offer training where possible. Teaching proper drying and storage reduces rejections and improves both parties' margins.
  • Sign simple written agreements covering volume, price, quality, and delivery dates. Even a one-page contract reduces disputes.
  • Diversify. Do not rely on one supplier. Two or three reliable sources protect you from drought, disease, or price shocks.

Storing Fresh Herbs to Maintain Quality

Poor storage destroys more value than poor harvesting. Herbs lose aroma, color, and medicinal compounds through heat, light, moisture, and oxygen. For a small business, storage is a direct profit lever: better storage means longer shelf life, fewer returns, and stronger brand reputation.

  • Dry thoroughly first. Herbs should be crisp, not leathery, before storage. Moisture causes mold and mycotoxins.
  • Use airtight containers. Glass jars, food-grade buckets with sealed lids, or vacuum bags. Avoid open sacks.
  • Store in a cool, dark, dry place. Ideal: below 25Â°C, away from sunlight, with low humidity.
  • Label everything. Include herb name, harvest date, supplier, and batch number.
  • Rotate stock. Use older batches first (FIFO). Review stock monthly for pests or moisture.
  • Keep samples. Retain a small sample of each batch for at least 6 months for traceability and quality disputes.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Identify every herb using at least two independent sources before harvesting or buying.
  2. Never harvest from roadsides, sprayed fields, or industrial areas.
  3. Confirm your supplier can name the species and source of every batch.
  4. Harvest no more than 30% of a wild plant population per season.
  5. Dry herbs thoroughly until crisp before storage.
  6. Store in airtight, labeled containers away from heat, light, and moisture.
  7. Keep batch samples for at least 6 months for traceability.
  8. Maintain written agreements and timely payments with all suppliers.
  9. Review stock monthly for pests, mold, or quality loss.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Non-Wood Forest Products: Medicinal Plants (free, official)
  • WHO â Guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) for Medicinal Plants (free, official)
  • CBI â Market Information for Natural Ingredients and Herbal Teas (free, official)
  • FAO â Quality Assurance of Herbal Medicines and Related Substances (free PDF)
  • African Clearing House â Traditional Medicine and Herbal Trade Resources (free, regional)

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Herbal Teas & Infusions. Always verify local regulations before harvesting, processing, or selling herbal products. When in doubt, consult a qualified botanist or agricultural extension officer.

quiz.q: Which part of the hibiscus plant is dried and brewed for tea?
quiz.explanation: Hibiscus tea is made from the fleshy red calyces, not the petals.

quiz.q: How long should rooibos be fermented to get its deep red colour?
quiz.explanation: Rooibos is fermented in heaps for 8 to 12 hours to develop colour and flavour.

quiz.q: What is the best way to dry moringa leaves to keep them green?
options: C) Shade dry for 2 to 3 days
D) Smoke them over a fire
quiz.explanation: Shade drying preserves the green colour and vitamins in moringa leaves.

quiz.q: How often can lemongrass be harvested from the same clump?
quiz.explanation: Lemongrass regrows quickly and can be cut every 6 to 8 weeks.

quiz.q: What is a safe water temperature for steeping moringa leaf tea?
quiz.explanation: Water at about 80 degrees Celsius preserves nutrients and prevents bitterness.

quiz.q: Which of these is a risk of wild harvesting?
quiz.explanation: Roadside plants can be contaminated by exhaust and herbicides.

quiz.q: What is the 'one in three' rule for wild harvesting?
options: A) Harvest three plants and leave one
B) Harvest one plant for every three you find
C) Harvest only three days a month
D) Sell one of every three baskets
quiz.explanation: The rule means taking only one plant out of every three to allow regrowth.

quiz.q: Why should you visit a farm before buying herbs?
options: A) To check crop quality and drying methods
D) To learn a new language
quiz.explanation: A farm visit lets you verify quality, drying, and harvest practices.

quiz.q: What should you bring when buying dried herbs at a market?
options: A) A moisture meter and clean container
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter and clean container help you check and protect quality.

quiz.q: Which smell indicates fresh dried lemongrass?
quiz.explanation: Fresh dried lemongrass should have a strong lemon aroma.

quiz.q: Which plant is a dangerous lookalike for some edible herbs?
quiz.explanation: Datura is highly poisonous and can be mistaken for other leafy plants.

quiz.q: What is the first step in identifying a new herb safely?
options: B) Confirm leaf shape and arrangement
D) Mix it with other herbs
quiz.explanation: Leaf shape and arrangement are the first reliable identification features.

quiz.q: How many experienced people should confirm a new plant before you harvest it?
quiz.explanation: Getting two confirmations reduces the risk of misidentification.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are not 100% sure a plant is safe?
options: C) Feed it to animals first
quiz.explanation: If unsure, discard the plant to avoid poisoning.

quiz.q: How much of a moringa tree can you harvest at one time?
quiz.explanation: Taking no more than one-third allows the tree to recover.

quiz.q: How high should you cut lemongrass stalks?
options: B) 15 to 20 cm above the ground
quiz.explanation: Cutting 15 to 20 cm above ground leaves the base to regrow.

quiz.q: Why should you not harvest rooibos from the same bush two years in a row?
options: A) The bush needs a rest period
B) The bush dies after one year
quiz.explanation: Rooibos bushes need a rest period to regrow healthy stems and leaves.

quiz.q: What tool is best for harvesting herbs sustainably?
options: B) Sharp secateurs or a knife
quiz.explanation: Sharp secateurs or a knife make clean cuts and reduce plant damage.

quiz.q: What should you record when harvesting wild herbs?
options: A) Date, location, herb, and amount
quiz.explanation: Recording date, location, herb, and amount helps rotate harvest sites.

quiz.q: Why is a 10 m by 10 m herb garden useful?
options: A) It reduces pressure on wild areas
quiz.explanation: A small garden can supply a business and reduce wild harvesting.

quiz.q: How should you treat a supplier you want to keep?
quiz.explanation: Treating suppliers as partners builds trust and reliable supply.

quiz.q: What is a good first step when meeting a new herb supplier?
options: B) Visit in person and listen
quiz.explanation: An in-person visit and listening build a strong relationship.

quiz.q: Why should you pay a deposit before harvest?
options: A) To secure supply and help the farmer
quiz.explanation: A deposit helps the farmer buy inputs and secures your supply.

quiz.q: How many suppliers should you have for each herb?
quiz.explanation: Having at least three suppliers protects you if one has a bad season.

quiz.q: What should you do if a supplier delivers poor quality herbs?
options: A) Discuss it calmly and agree on a solution
C) Never speak to them again
quiz.explanation: Calm discussion preserves the relationship and improves future quality.

quiz.q: What is the correct moisture level for dried herbs?
quiz.explanation: Dried herbs should have less than 10 percent moisture to prevent mould.

quiz.q: How do you know a herb is fully dry?
quiz.explanation: A fully dry herb snaps cleanly instead of bending.

quiz.q: What container is best for storing small quantities of dried herbs?
options: B) Glass jars with airtight lids
quiz.explanation: Airtight glass jars protect herbs from air and moisture.

quiz.q: What is the first-in, first-out rule?
options: A) Sell older stock before newer stock
quiz.explanation: Selling older stock first prevents spoilage and waste.

quiz.q: How long can properly stored dried hibiscus and rooibos last?
quiz.explanation: Hibiscus and rooibos can keep quality for up to 2 years if stored dry and dark.
